lessons.title: Lesson 1: Main point first: clear work messages
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a work message with the main point first and a clear ask.
This lesson builds toward: Given a message you need to send at work, you will write the message with the main point first and a clear ask with a deadline, covering one topic, with every fact checked.
Busy people read the first line and skim the rest. Put the main point or the ask first, then the details, then what you need and by when. Example: "Can you cover my Saturday 8-4 shift? I have a family emergency. Please reply by Thursday noon."
Keep it short: one topic per message, short sentences, bullet points for lists. Use a clear subject line for email: "Need cover: Sat 8-4 shift".
An AI assistant can turn rough notes into a clear message: "Rewrite this so the main point is first, under 80 words, polite and direct." You check the facts, names and times.
Step by step:
- Write the main point or ask in one sentence.
- Add only the details the reader needs.
- Say what you need and by when.
- Use a clear subject line.
- Ask AI to tighten it, then check facts.
Words to know:
- Main point first: putting the most important message or request at the start.
- Subject line: the short title of an email.
Try it now: Take a message you need to send (or a sample, like asking for a schedule change). Rewrite it main point first with a deadline, ask AI to tighten it, and check every fact.
You can now write a short work message with the main point and ask first.

check.q: Why put the main point first in a work message?
options: Busy people read the first line and skim the rest
check.why: Readers who only see the first line still get what you need.

check.q: You need Friday off. Which message do you send?
options: "Can I have Friday off for a medical appointment? Please let me know by Wednesday."
"Hi, hope you are well, so this week has been busy and..."
A message with three different requests
check.why: It puts the ask first, gives a reason and a deadline, and covers one topic.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Handoffs that do not drop anything
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Give a complete shift or task handoff using a simple checklist.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of a shift or task, you will give a complete handoff using the five-section checklist, with open items and what to watch for, and no private details in unapproved tools.
Many problems at work happen at handoffs: end of shift, a coworker going on leave, a task passed to someone else. A short checklist keeps things from falling through.
A good handoff covers: Status (where things stand), Open items (what is not finished), Watch for (risks or problems), Contacts (who to call), and Next steps (what the next person should do first).
You can speak your notes into your phone or type them quickly and ask AI: "Turn these notes into a handoff with sections Status, Open items, Watch for, Contacts, Next steps." Leave out private customer, patient or employee details unless you are using an approved work system.
Step by step:
- Write or speak rough notes at the end of the shift or task.
- Organize into Status, Open items, Watch for, Contacts, Next steps.
- Check nothing is missing.
- Hand it over and answer questions.
Words to know:
- Handoff: passing work to another person, with the information they need.
- Open item: something not finished yet.
Try it now: Write a handoff for your current or last job (or a sample warehouse shift) using the five sections. Use AI to organize your rough notes and check nothing is missing.
You can now give a complete handoff so the next person knows what to do.

options: Many problems happen when work changes hands
check.why: Information gets lost when work changes hands, so a checklist keeps it complete.

check.q: You are handing off a shift and a pallet is leaning badly. Where does it go?
options: Nowhere; the next person will see it
In a text to a friend
check.why: Safety issues and things to watch go in the handoff so the next person acts on them.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Status updates and asking for help
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Send a short status update and ask for help early and clearly.
This lesson builds toward: Each week, or when you are stuck, you will write a Done / Next / Blocked status update and ask for help early, with what you tried, what you need and by when.
Managers like to hear progress before they have to ask. A three-line update works: Done (what you finished), Next (what you are doing next), Blocked (what is stopping you and what you need).
Ask for help early, not at the deadline. Say what you tried, what you need, and by when: "I tried resetting the scanner and checking the cable. It still won't connect. Can IT look at it before 2 pm?"
AI can help you find the words when a message feels awkward, like asking for more time or telling your manager about a mistake. Keep it honest and short.
Step by step:
- Write Done, Next, Blocked.
- For any block, say what you tried and what you need.
- Send it before you are asked.
- Ask for help early with a clear deadline.
Words to know:
- Status update: a short report on progress.
- Blocked: unable to continue until something is fixed or someone helps.
Try it now: Write a Done / Next / Blocked update for this week (real or sample). Include one clear request for help with what you tried and a deadline.
You can now send clear status updates and ask for help early.

check.q: What does "Blocked" mean in a status update?
options: You cannot continue until something is fixed
check.why: Blocked tells your manager what is stopping you so they can help.

check.q: You have been stuck on a task for a day and it is due tomorrow. What do you do?
options: Keep trying alone and say nothing
Ask for help now, saying what you tried, what you need and by when
check.why: Asking early with details gives others time to help before the deadline.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Getting the right work done

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Sorting your to-do list: urgent vs important
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort tasks into four boxes and decide what to do first.
This lesson builds toward: Given at least ten tasks, you will sort them into the four urgent and important boxes and choose your top three, asking your manager when you are unsure what comes first.
When everything feels urgent, sort it. Draw four boxes: Urgent and important (do now), Important not urgent (schedule it), Urgent not important (delegate or do quickly), Neither (drop or later). This is often called the Eisenhower matrix.
Important tasks connect to your goals or your job's main duties: safety, customers, deadlines your manager set. Urgent tasks have a close deadline or someone waiting.
You can paste your to-do list (without confidential details) into AI and ask it to suggest boxes. Then decide yourself: you know what your manager expects. When unsure, ask your manager which comes first.
Step by step:
- List all your tasks.
- Ask: is it important? Is it urgent?
- Put each in one of the four boxes.
- Do box 1, schedule box 2, hand off or speed through box 3, drop box 4.
- When unsure, ask your manager.
Words to know:
- Urgent: needs attention soon, with a close deadline or someone waiting.
- Important: connected to your main duties or goals.
- Eisenhower matrix: a four-box way to sort tasks by urgent and important.
Try it now: List at least ten tasks for this week. Sort them into the four boxes (ask AI for a first try if you like), then pick your top three for tomorrow.
You can now sort a to-do list by urgent and important and choose what to do first.

options: It connects to your main duties, safety or goals
check.why: Important tasks connect to your main duties, safety and goals.

check.q: A task is not urgent and not important. What do you do with it?
options: Ask a coworker to do it right now
Drop it or do it later
check.why: Box 4 tasks are dropped or done later so time goes to what matters.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Planning your week with time blocks
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a week by blocking time for important work.
This lesson builds toward: For next week, you will create a time-blocked plan with your shifts, important tasks, message blocks and buffer time, adjusted to your real life.
A to-do list says what; a calendar says when. Time blocking means putting tasks into set times on your calendar, such as "Tuesday 9-10: finish inventory report".
Block your important-but-not-urgent tasks first, because they get pushed aside. Add short blocks for email and messages instead of checking all day. Leave some open time for surprises.
Ask AI: "Here are my shifts and my tasks with time estimates. Make a time-blocked plan for next week with buffer time." Then adjust it to your real life: commute, family, breaks.
Step by step:
- Write your fixed times: shifts, meetings, family.
- Estimate how long each task takes.
- Block important tasks first.
- Add short message blocks and buffer time.
- Ask AI for a draft and adjust it.
Words to know:
- Time blocking: putting tasks into set times on your calendar.
- Buffer time: open time left for surprises and delays.
Try it now: Make a time-blocked plan for next week with your shifts, three important tasks, two message blocks and buffer time. Use AI for a first draft if you like.
You can now plan a week with time blocks so important work gets done.

options: Open time in your plan for surprises and delays
check.why: Buffer time keeps a surprise from wrecking the whole plan.

check.q: The AI's weekly plan puts a task during your Tuesday shift. What do you do?
options: Move it to a time that fits your real schedule
check.why: AI drafts the plan, but you adjust it to your real life.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Using AI as a helper, not a replacement
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI for the right parts of your work and keep your judgment in charge.
This lesson builds toward: When you use AI to help with your work, you will choose which parts AI drafts and check every fact before sending, using only approved tools and keeping confidential data out.
AI helps most with first drafts, organizing notes, summarizing, and finding words for hard messages. It does not know your workplace, your coworkers or what your manager really meant, and it can be wrong.
Good habits: give it your notes, not your thinking; ask for a short draft; check every fact; make it sound like you; follow your workplace AI rules; keep confidential and personal information out.
Track one thing: time saved. If a tool saves you 20 minutes a day on messages, that is time for the people part of your job, which is where you stand out.
Step by step:
- Use AI for drafts, organizing and summaries.
- Check facts and make it sound like you.
- Follow workplace AI rules.
- Note the time you save each week.
Words to know:
- Judgment: your ability to decide well using what you know.
Try it now: Final task: build your one-week kit: one main-point-first message, one handoff, one Done/Next/Blocked update, a four-box to-do list and a time-blocked week. Use AI to draft at least two and check every fact.
You can now communicate clearly and manage your time at work with AI as a helper.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Main-point-first message The main point or ask is buried or missing. The main point is first, with a clear ask and a deadline, on one topic. Has a clear subject line, and the message is under 100 words. Complete handoff One or more of the five sections is missing. All five sections, including open items and what to watch for. Each open item says who owns it next. Status update Missing Done, Next or Blocked. A Done / Next / Blocked update with one clear request for help. The help request says what was tried and by when it is needed. Four-box list and time blocks Tasks are not sorted, or the week has no time blocks. Ten tasks in the four boxes and a week with shifts, three important tasks, message blocks and buffer time. Important but not urgent tasks are blocked first. AI checked AI drafts were sent without checking, or private details were used. AI helped draft at least two items, and every fact was checked. The learner notes one fact they corrected. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which part of your work is AI good at?
check.why: AI helps with drafts and organizing; judgment and people work stay with you.

check.q: You want AI to clean up notes that include a patient's name. What do you do?
options: Paste them into any free AI
Use only an approved tool, or remove the private details first
Email them to a friend to fix
check.why: Workplace rules come first: approved tools only, and confidential data stays out.
